contentTest.audience: The principal of a small Madison-area residential design studio who is adding her first designer or assistant while the workload doubles, and who walks the Fall Parade to see how other studios' houses came together (VISION §2: the studio is the customer; homeowners and makers are the studio's clients and vendors, never the reader we ask anything of).
contentTest.moment: Fall Parade weekends, October 9–11 and 16–18, 2026: she is standing in someone else's finished rooms (the Moll Drive house, Leah's interiors, Kippley's build) wondering how the job actually ran and whether her own studio could carry one like it with a new hire. Surface: The Document (VISION §1 #1), introduced as the page the next job runs from.
contentTest.promise: You won't notice Patina (VISION §4, to the studio): one living page per client, from brief to install, that a new hire and a builder's crew can work from without the owner retelling the job. No engagement ask, no dashboards; the one ask is a conversation with Leah and an application to the Founding 50 with one live project.
contentTest.reason: Passes the feature test on all four counts: surface = The Document; studio moment = the first-hire year, met where the principal already is (the Parade); stream = the studio subscription (the floor); promise = you won't notice Patina. Acquisition is 1:1 through Leah's network (her email, her presence at the house, her leave-behind), not SEO strangers. No Pledge language, no held tagline, no prices or time-saved figures. Parade visitors (homeowners) will read P04 and P07, but those pieces only describe the house and honor Kippley's craft; their sole ask is to designers. The house itself was NOT run in Patina; every piece says it is the kind of job Patina is being built for, the next one. The one risk held open is honesty: C30 (Leah's day and hours) stays ⟨FILL⟩ and no piece may imply the crew, Leah or a client used a Patina page.

concept.name: Every room began as a brief
concept.idea: Studios walk the Parade to see finished rooms and never see the job behind them: the brief, the sample board, the drawing, the question from the site. The Moll Drive house is Leah's work, built by a Sauk City crew that frames, finishes and builds its own millwork. The batch tells that honestly: this house ran the way most studios run a house (NOT on Patina); the next one runs from one living page per client, from brief to install, that a new hire or a builder's crew can pick up. Three angles from the brief, one per surface: the decisions you can't see from the doorway (P01, P04, P07), the warm wood and the crew behind it (P02), and a studio owner talking to another studio owner in a finished kitchen (P03, P05, P06). Direction and copy come from the seed copy; rivals may improve wording only.
concept.artDirection: Real, credited photographs of the Moll Drive house, no people, daylight through real windows: a room from the doorway, the woodwork's grain up close, the front of the house in late afternoon. Paper ground (#EDE9E4), Playfair Display headlines in sentence case, Inter body, DM Mono eyebrow carrying the place and date line (Waunakee · Fall Parade · Oct 16–18). Instagram: image owns the top two thirds, headline on paper below. Poster: one image, one Playfair line readable from six feet; J04 is the only image that may be generated (a warm oak and brass texture, an illustration never captioned as the house) and it may be swapped for a real detail photo. One-pagers: eyebrow, Playfair title, one image band, three or four single-column sections, CTA at the foot, print-safe. Email: letter first, at most one photo under the opening paragraph, readable with images off. Flat paper, ink and clay-beige hairlines; no gradients, no badges, no red/green.
